newsitem.title: USA: Developers, green groups clash on wetlands plan.
newsitem.headline: Developers, green groups clash on wetlands plan.

text.p: Land developers Thursday said the Clinton Administration's plan to rein in their ability to drain small wetlands areas will increase costs for some housing and development.

Environmentalists on the other hand applauded the plan. But they said the Army Corps of Engineers was taking too long to revamp its wetlands permit programme, and they worried its new plan would leave too many loopholes for developers.

The Corps later Thursday was formally to unveil its plan to phase out the Nation 26 permit programme, under which landowners could get permits to develop up to 10 acres of wetlands with minimal government review or interference.
The permits have been used for isolated or headwaters wetlands, not expanses along river bottoms and coastal areas.
The lower 48 states have lost about half their wetlands -- important for wildlife habitat, flood control and water quality -- to development.

Corps officials said for the next two years, they will put tighter constraints on the permits and reduce the size of wetland plots that will come under careful government scrutiny to at least 3 acres from at least 10 acres. Plans to develop wetlands of at least one-third acre also would come under review, down from the current one acre.
After two years, the Corps is to have a new system for small wetlands which will give permit applications more individual review, and base permits on the type of proposed development.

"The effect of that will be to increase the time it takes to get a decision from the government, which will increase costs," said Michael Luzier, the National Association of Home Builders' assistant staff vice president for environmental regulations.
"I can't tell you how much it will raise houses' costs, x or y," but Luzier said the additional required lead time on projects will be factored into final costs.

Environmental groups, who have long complained that the current programme has allowed destruction of thousands of acres of small but environmentally important wetlands, said they were pleased by the administration's plan.

"The Nationwide Permit 26 was the most destructive general permit and probably the majority of wetlands destruction authorised by the Corps has taken place under it," John Echeverria, the National Audubon Society's general counsel, said. "This is a modest step in the direction of greater balance in this programme."

But environmentalists said the plan should require more reviews by other resource agencies, such as the Fish and Wildlife Service, which often show more environmental concern than the Corps. It also should give states the right to reject Corps development permits to protect their water quality.

Luzier said homebuilders and other developers will take their case to Congress, arguing that the administration's plan contradicts legislation Congress passed in 1977 to streamline the permitting programme.

But Echeverria, of the National Audubon Society, said: "Ten acres represents seven-and-a-half football fields. The idea that is always going to have minimal impacts is not defensible, and I think it's unlikely Congress will overrule the change."
